title: The vote must remain sealed
text: Once a citizen is already eligible to participate, one essential requirement still remains: the decision itself must stay private. That is where commitments matter.

title: What is a commitment
text: A cryptographic commitment is a primitive that allows you to 'seal' a value. The book defines it as: commit(value) → commitment. Later, you can open it to reveal the original value. Properties: hiding (can't see value) and binding (can't change value after committing).
visualHint: Lock box containing a secret value

title: The two properties
text: The book emphasizes: (1) Hiding - the commitment doesn't reveal the value. (2) Binding - once committed, you can't change what you committed to. These two properties make commitments fundamental to privacy-preserving protocols.
visualHint: Shield for hiding, chains for binding

title: Commitments in Midnight
text: Midnight provides two primitives: persistentCommit and persistentHash. The book explains these are stored in the ledger and provide the foundation for private data handling. Understanding them is key to building on Midnight.
visualHint: Two different types of commit boxes in the ledger

title: persistentCommit: the sealed value
text: The book explains that persistentCommit stores a value that can only be revealed by the holder of the opening key. Think of it as a safe deposit box: only the owner can open it. It's perfect for vote encryption and token amounts.

title: persistentHash: the public summary
text: persistentHash is different. It creates a verifiable fingerprint for data that should not be exposed in full. In this story, it is useful for public summaries such as the root of a protected electoral register.
visualHint: Fingerprint scanner showing a hash output

title: When to use each
text: The book gives clear guidance: use persistentCommit for values that must remain hidden until revealed (votes, amounts). Use persistentHash for data that's public but needs integrity (Merkle roots, public announcements). The choice affects privacy.
visualHint: Decision tree: hidden until reveal → persistentCommit; public integrity → persistentHash

title: The opening key
text: persistentCommit uses a two-part system: the commitment and an opening key. The book explains that only someone with the opening key can reveal the value. This enables selective disclosure - you can prove something about a value without revealing it all.
visualHint: Key opening a lock to reveal value

title: The register must exist without being exposed
text: After identity and civic conditions are validated, eligible citizens must belong to an electoral register. The challenge is proving membership without publishing the full list.
visualHint: Protected electoral register inside a secure structure

title: What is a Merkle tree
text: A Merkle tree is a binary tree where each leaf is a hash of data, and each parent is the hash of its children's hashes. The book shows that the root is a compact representation of all data. Changing any leaf changes the root.
visualHint: Binary tree with leaves at bottom, root at top

title: Merkle proof of membership
text: To prove membership, you provide the leaf value and the sibling hashes along the path to the root. The verifier can recompute the root from these. The book emphasizes: the proof size is O(log n), efficient for large sets.
visualHint: Path highlighted from leaf to root with sibling hashes

title: Using Merkle trees in circuits
text: The book shows how to verify Merkle proofs in a circuit. The circuit takes the leaf, the proof path, and recomputes the root. This is how privacy-preserving eligibility verification works: prove you're in the set without revealing which element you are.

title: Application: verifiable electoral register
text: The election authority publishes a Merkle root of the eligible register. Each citizen presents a membership proof and the system confirms access without revealing full identity.
visualHint: Voting registration with Merkle tree verification

title: Application: token balance verification
text: For private token transfers, commitments represent token amounts. The book explains that a Merkle tree can store commitment openings, and proofs verify sufficient balance without revealing the exact amount or the user's identity.
visualHint: Token balance tree with proof verification

title: The full flow
text: The book summarizes: (1) Commit to value with persistentCommit. (2) Store commitment in ledger. (3) For verification, use ZK circuit with Merkle proof. (4) The verifier checks commitment + proof without seeing values.
visualHint: Flow diagram: commit → store → prove → verify

title: Putting it together
text: The book concludes by showing how commitments and Merkle trees are the backbone of privacy on Midnight. They enable proving properties about private data while keeping the data hidden. Master these, and you can build any private application.
visualHint: Architecture diagram showing all pieces connected
